week.t: NASA Earth Observatory: Navajo Reservoir rose nearly 60 feet between 20 September and 7 November, to 108% of average
NASA invites the public to flash VGR in Morse code at Voyager 1 on 17 November, the eve of its one-light-day mark
Science News Explores: a 14-year-old piloted a borrowed ROV over six California kelp beds and found few urchins
NASA: the station crew packs a Dragon cargo craft with microbe samples and a spacesuit for return next week
NASA: Perseverance’s SuperCam traces glows at 692.7 and 694.1 nm to chromium in corundum, the ruby family

tiles.cap: Voyager 1 is one light-day away next week. NASA wants your phone to flash it on Tuesday
tiles.nums: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km) from Earth: light, and any radio command, now takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 18 November, NASA says, Voyager 1 will have travelled one light-day from Earth: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km), so far that light from Earth takes 24 hours to reach it. The evening before, Tuesday 17 November, NASA is asking people everywhere to make a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset, “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day”. A NASA web page makes a phone or tablet flash VGR, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA announced the activities on Tuesday 10 November. A panel from JPL is streamed on NASA’s site on Friday 20 November at 1 am Singapore time (Thursday noon US Eastern).
deep: Who is talking

The discussion at JPL’s von Kármán Auditorium in Southern California includes Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science; Jonathan Lunine, JPL’s chief scientist; Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager; and Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, the deputy project scientist. It takes questions and is streamed live.
A film is coming
NASA says the event previews a Voyager documentary on NASA+ planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
Which day, exactly

NASA’s invitation says the one-light-day mark falls on Wednesday 18 November, with the light activation the evening before; NASA’s November skywatching page lists the milestone on 17 November. Its chart puts Voyager 1 in the constellation Ophiuchus, toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on the 17th: you cannot see the probe, but you can face it.
Where the picture comes from
The image is an artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft from NASA/JPL-Caltech; no camera is out there to photograph it.
tiles.src: NASA release M26-086, 10 Nov 2026 (Gerelle Q. Dodson): NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities · NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn on Tuesday and Wednesday, up to 15 an hour. Tonight, the Taurids
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 17 and 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Tonight, 12 November, the Northern Taurids peak at a gentler 5 an hour. And on the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stand about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November (US Pacific time); NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way
NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm, the day it is a light-day away.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Perseverance’s laser lit two reds in a Mars rock, 692.7 and 694.1 nm: ruby’s glow
tiles.nums: and 694.1 nanometres: the two luminescence peaks SuperCam saw, traced to chromium in corundum, the mineral family that includes ruby
tiles.p1: When Perseverance’s SuperCam fires its laser at a rock, some rocks glow back. Roger Wiens of Purdue University, SuperCam’s principal investigator, writes that luminescence peaks at 692.7 and 694.1 nanometres have been traced to chromium sitting in corundum, the mineral family that includes ruby. “While we haven’t found collectable rubies on Mars yet,” he writes, the find is reported in Geophysical Research Letters in a paper led by Ann Ollila.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA posted the blog on Monday 9 November (written 4 November). The team thinks the corundum may come from localised metamorphism in large impacts near the rim of Jezero crater.
deep: The laser as a lamp

SuperCam’s luminescence measurement reads the light a rock gives off after the laser hits it; the exact wavelengths act like a fingerprint of the atoms inside. Here the fingerprint was chromium inside corundum.
Why that matters
Corundum needs particular conditions to form. Wiens’ team suggests metamorphism driven by large impacts near the crater rim, where the rover has been exploring.
The rock in the picture

NASA’s image shows “Nhlanguleni”, a heavily pitted, light-toned float rock, photographed by the WATSON camera on the rover’s SHERLOC instrument on Sol 2023, 29 October 2026, at a spot called “Kapama Karula” in the “South Idubi” region.
In his words
“Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected,” Wiens writes.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Perseverance rover blog: Rubies on Mars? (Roger C. Wiens, Purdue University), posted 9 Nov 2026 · Geophysical Research Letters (Ollila et al.)

tiles.cap: A reservoir rose nearly 60 feet in seven weeks. Landsat watched the desert lake refill
tiles.nums: nearly 60 feet (18 m) of rise at Navajo Reservoir between 20 September and 7 November 2026, from 60% to 108% of average for the date
tiles.p1: Two Landsat 9 images, taken on 20 September and 7 November 2026, show Navajo Reservoir on the New Mexico–Colorado border swelling after weeks of rain. US Army Corps of Engineers data say the lake rose nearly 60 feet (18 m) between the two dates, from 60 percent of average for the date to 108 percent, its highest since August 2019. The cause: back-to-back extreme rain events over the Four Corners region in late October and early November, with precipitation from early September to early November two to four times the average.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA Earth Observatory’s image of the day for Wednesday 11 November, after a “snow drought” winter had left the lake low.
deep: One storm, five inches

Pagosa Springs, Colorado, about 40 miles (64 km) northeast of the lake, on the San Juan River, got 5.05 inches (12.8 cm) of rain in the first storm. The river reached major flood stage on 23 October and nearly matched its 1911 record on 1 November; evacuation orders were issued and dozens of people were rescued.
Drought over, for now
The US Drought Monitor said on 3 November that short-term drought had ended for the Southwest and Great Basin. The 2025–26 snowpack had been so low that the spring melt gave the reservoir little.
Why so wet
Earth Observatory links the weather to El Niño and to a low-latitude low-pressure system fed by unusually warm ocean temperatures.
The eyes
The Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9; images by Michala Garrison, story by Lindsey Doermann.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day, 11 Nov 2026: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir (Lindsey Doermann; images Michala Garrison, Landsat data from USGS)
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, Landsat 9 data from USGS

tiles.cap: An IISc drone flies beside a blind walker and places obstacles to within 25 cm
tiles.nums: how closely the drone judged the distance to the person it followed; cars and bicycles within 60 cm, where existing depth software was off by 1.4 to 2 m
tiles.p1: A smart cane only finds what is straight ahead. Yogesh Simmhan’s group at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru wants a small drone flying alongside a visually impaired person, warning of obstacles around them. The catch: a cheap drone has one camera, and a single camera cannot easily tell whether an object is small and close or big and far away. Their method, NeoARCADE, turns a camera’s depth scores into real distances: on the IISc campus it judged the distance to the person it followed to within 25 cm, and to cars and bicycles within 60 cm.
tiles.p2: Why here: more than 2.2 billion people worldwide have some form of visual impairment, the IISc page says; the paper is in ACM Transactions on Cyber-Physical Systems (2026).
deep: Teach it a ruler

Existing depth-map software only ranks nearer and farther. Here the user first stands at a few known distances from the drone; the system derives a rule linking depth score to distance, then applies it to other objects using each object’s pixel closest to the camera. When conditions change it detects the drift and recalibrates.
In the field

Testing, led by doctoral student Suman Raj, used a small off-the-shelf drone following a student posing as a visually impaired person around campus, with the computing done on a small GPU device that fits in a backpack.
The numbers
Within 25 cm for the person, 60 cm for cars and bicycles; the existing depth-map software was off by 1.4 to 2 m.
Who
Simmhan is in IISc’s Department of Computational and Data Sciences; the authors are Raj, Madhabhavi, Kumar, Gupta and Simmhan.
tiles.src: Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru (Mohit Singh): Helping drones guide visually impaired people, 2026 · ACM Transactions on Cyber-Physical Systems (Raj et al., 2026)

tiles.cap: A motor from 60 cm of wire, 2 magnets, 2 paper clips and a battery. Trick: one black mark
tiles.nums: of solid copper wire (20–24 gauge), wound into a 2.5 cm coil of four or five loops, is enough for the Exploratorium’s stripped-down motor
tiles.p1: The Exploratorium’s stripped-down motor is a coil of wire about 2.5 cm across, resting in two unfolded paper clips above a ceramic magnet, with a C or D battery wired in through strips of aluminium foil. Flick it and it spins. When current flows the coil becomes an electromagnet with a north face and a south face; the magnet below pulls the opposite pole and pushes the like one, so the coil turns. Equivalently, Feynman’s force law says a magnetic field pushes sideways on moving charges, and the current in the top and bottom of the loop is pushed in opposite directions: a twist.
tiles.p2: Why it keeps going: one projecting wire end is painted black on half its circumference, so the current cuts out for half of every turn, the coil never settles, and inertia carries it round to the next push.
deep: Build it

Wind four or five loops; wrap each wire end round the coil to hold it, leaving about 5 cm sticking out each side; strip the insulation or sand the enamel off the ends. Set the coil so it clears the magnet by about 1.5 mm (1/16 in). Stack a second magnet inside the cup under the first to strengthen the field.
If it will not spin

Check the coil is balanced, the enamel fully removed, exactly one end half-painted, and the coil clears the magnet. The Exploratorium says to be patient: the design has a high success rate. Then reverse the battery, add a second, or flip the magnets and watch what changes.
The real thing

The sliding contacts are commutators. Real DC motors use commutators that reverse the current every half-turn instead of just cutting it, which makes them about twice as powerful as this design. Swap the battery for a sensitive galvanometer, spin the coil by hand, and it becomes a generator.
Feynman’s one line

In Volume II, chapter 1, the whole of electromagnetism’s push on a charge is one formula: the electric field pushes any charge, the magnetic field pushes only a moving charge, and sideways to its motion. The motor is that second term, made of paper clips.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Stripped-Down Motor · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, ch. 1 (Caltech)

tiles.cap: Air molecules hit your hand at about 500 m/s, all day. You feel nothing. Here is why
tiles.nums: the average speed of air molecules at 300 K (25 °C), about 1,100 mph, says NIST; individual molecules vary, 223 m/s and 717 m/s among its examples
tiles.p1: At 300 K, about 25 °C, the molecules of air move at an average of about 500 m/s, around 1,100 mph, according to NIST, the US standards institute; some go at 223 m/s, others at 717 m/s, in every direction. Feynman’s lecture on the kinetic theory of gases turns that pummelling into pressure: each molecule bouncing off a wall hands it a small kick of momentum, and adding up the kicks per second gives a pressure equal to two-thirds of the molecules’ kinetic energy per unit volume. You feel none of it because it comes from all sides at once.
tiles.p2: Test it with the Exploratorium’s Bernoulli levitator: push a pin through a 7.5 cm square of card, hold it under a thread spool with the pin up the hole, blow hard down through the spool and let go. The card hangs on.
deep: The one-third

Molecules move randomly in all directions, so on average the motion splits equally between the three directions of space; only the share aimed at the wall counts, which is where the 1/3 in Feynman’s formula comes from. Only half the molecules near the wall are heading toward it, and that half cancels the factor 2 in each bounce, so the final formula has no stray twos.
Temperature is speed

Feynman defines temperature so that the average kinetic energy of a molecule is 3/2 kT, with Boltzmann’s constant k. Two different gases at the same temperature have the same average energy per molecule, so the lighter molecules move faster. k was fixed at exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin when the kelvin was redefined in November 2018, NIST explains.
Why the card hangs

Air leaving the spool spreads fast across the card; the Exploratorium says any fluid loses pressure as it speeds up, so the fast layer between spool and card is at lower pressure than the still air below, and the still air pushes the card up against the spool. The same effect works an atomizer and can pop windows out when two trains pass.
Light has pressure too
Feynman adds that a gas of light, photons, pushes with one-third of its energy per volume rather than two-thirds.
tiles.src: NIST, SI Redefinition: Kelvin — Boltzmann Constant · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 39 (Caltech) · Exploratorium Science Snacks: Bernoulli Levitator

tiles.cap: A $100 kids’ landline: cord, no screen, no apps, Wi-Fi inside. One 7-year-old shrugged
tiles.nums: a month for Tin Can’s Party Line plan, which lets approved ordinary phone numbers call in; Tin Can to Tin Can calls are free
tiles.p1: Tin Can looks like an old desk phone with a curly cord, and that is the point: no screen, no apps, no texting, no games, no internet. Inside it is a Wi-Fi device: it runs on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, plugs into a wall socket, needs no phone line and, as Tom’s Guide’s Mike Prospero explains, makes its calls with VoIP, voice carried over the internet. Only people a parent approves in the companion app can call it or be called; 911 emergency calls are always on. TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list, noting that some 106 countries and 39 US states now restrict phones in schools.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the engineering is deliberately less. The question is whether a phone that can do only one thing stays interesting.
deep: What is inside

A Wi-Fi radio and a VoIP stack, a speakerphone, voicemail with a greeting you record yourself, speed dial and calling hours set in the app. Prospero compares the idea to MagicJack, the internet-phone gadget of years ago. Tin Can does not publish the handset’s weight or materials. A wired model, Flashback, takes an Ethernet cable instead of Wi-Fi.
The month-long test

Prospero gave one to his 7-year-old. Call quality was “good, but not great”; several voicemails were “crackly, which made them hard to understand”; voicemails can only be heard on the phone, not in the app; and after a month “the novelty of the Tin Can wore off pretty quickly”, and when he suggested calling a friend “she sort of just shrugs.” One parent told him the cords are “waaaaay too easy to unplug.”
The blue-bubble problem

A Tin Can cannot call a child who has a rival kids’ phone such as Pinwheel or Ring Ring: “It’s like a more exclusive version of the blue bubble,” Prospero writes. Tin Can to Tin Can is free; calls with ordinary numbers need the $9.99-a-month Party Line plan, with one free month included.
The maker’s line

“Tech made for kids doesn’t have to be addictive to be useful,” says Tin Can’s About page; the company, Tin Can Untechnologies, is in Seattle. A see-through Technicaller Clear edition with a light-up ringer costs $125.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Emma Barker Bonomo) · tincan.kids product and About pages · Tom’s Guide (Mike Prospero), updated 19 Jul 2026, one-month test

tiles.cap: NTU’s AI steers planes round moving thunderstorms. In the busiest tests, none got close
tiles.nums: of eight aircraft reached their goal in the same storms where four aircraft scored 100%; in the most crowded tests separation between planes was never lost
tiles.p1: Thunderstorms force controllers to reroute planes, and climate change is bringing more severe weather, writes NTU’s engineering school. The team of Associate Professor Sameer Alam, director of NTU’s Air Traffic Management Research Institute, built a cooperative AI, with the unlovely name IDDPG, a multi-agent framework that keeps aircraft a safe distance from thunderstorm cells and from each other while minimising total flight distance. In a 200 by 200 nautical mile box with two storm cells drifting northwest to southeast over 30 minutes, four aircraft from three entry points all got through safely; with eight aircraft the goal-reach rate fell to 95 percent and flight distances grew slightly.
tiles.p2: Why here: the test airspace was a real en route area of the Singapore flight information region, the sky our controllers manage.
deep: Pushing it

“We wanted to push the model to its limits,” Alam says. In six scenarios from one small cell to three large moving cells, performance declined as complexity rose and improved when storm tracks were known in advance. In the most crowded scenarios the goal-reach rate stayed at 98 to 99 percent and separation was never lost.
The weak spot
Uncertainty about when each plane arrives. The team tested four levels of estimated-time-of-arrival uncertainty, from negligible to high, and high uncertainty significantly degraded performance.
Why not one brain

Existing automation tools, the team says, are not scalable or efficient enough for fast-changing weather, and a single-agent approach limits cooperative decisions. “Our aim is to find an optimal solution to ensure safe separation distance among multiple aircraft,” Alam says.
Where it is published

Advanced Engineering Informatics 2025 (Pang, Hu, Zhang, Alam, Lulli) and the AAMAS 2026 conference on autonomous agents in Paphos, Cyprus. The article appeared on NTU’s mechanical and aerospace engineering news page on 4 November.
tiles.src: NTU School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering news, 4 Nov 2026: Artificial Intelligence Keeps Planes Safe in Bad Weather (MAE Collective 2026, AI edition) · Advanced Engineering Informatics 65:103157 (2025)

tiles.cap: Hold two combs a finger-width apart and slide one. The rippling pattern is not in them
tiles.nums: from a mirror: one comb and its reflection make the pattern too
tiles.p1: Hold two identical pocket combs about a finger’s width apart, look through them, and slide or turn one. Bands of light and dark ripple across; the Exploratorium says the pattern magnifies the slightest misalignment. The Exploratorium calls them moiré patterns: dark where the teeth of one comb cover the gaps of the other, light where the gaps line up. Only one comb? Hold it about 2.5 cm from a mirror and look at it together with its reflection.
tiles.p2: Why it works: the pattern is in the image your eye forms, not in the combs. It magnifies tiny misalignments: perfectly aligned, no pattern; more misaligned, the bands get thinner and closer together.
deep: Bigger versions

Two pieces of window screen overlapped and flexed; or one screen, a light and a white card moved away, so the screen and its own shadow make the pattern. Two transparencies printed with concentric circles, moved apart and together, give a pattern that looks like the nodal lines of a two-slit interference pattern, where light waves from the two slits cancel.
Spot it outside
Chain-link fences seen through each other, thin curtains folded double, and layers of fine fabric all show moiré.
Why it magnifies
Perfect alignment gives no pattern at all, and the greater the misalignment, the thinner and closer the bands, which is why the slightest misalignment shows up as a large, easily visible pattern.

tiles.cap: A 14-year-old borrowed a sea robot, got seasick at the controls, surveyed 6 kelp beds
tiles.nums: two declining, two recovering, two stable, chosen from Kelpwatch satellite data off Santa Cruz, California
tiles.p1: Linden Hunter-Pinsky, 14, passes kelp beds on his way to school in Santa Cruz, California. The state’s kelp declined sharply in the 2010s, due to a heat wave and other factors, and some beds near Santa Cruz are recovering while others are not. He used Kelpwatch satellite data to pick six beds, two declining, two recovering and two stable, borrowed a remotely operated vehicle from a local nonprofit, and piloted it from his family’s rowboat. “I was being jostled around by the waves while staring at this controller, and I got seasick,” he told Science News Explores.
tiles.p2: Why now: the project, done while he was at Gateway Middle School, made him a finalist in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge; the article ran on Tuesday 10 November.
deep: What the camera saw
None of the six beds had many sea urchins, which graze on kelp. He would “love to look more into other factors that might be preventing kelp forest recovery in certain places.”
Why kelp matters
Kelp forests shelter many species, including endangered ones, and trap climate-warming carbon.
Next
He is living in Chile for a year and is considering extending the project to Chile’s kelp forests. His advice: “Don’t feel constrained by what you think is a good project.”
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 10 Nov 2026 (Maria Temming), on Linden Hunter-Pinsky’s kelp-forest ROV survey

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, doing 48% better on the problems. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: the researchers say the students used the bot as a “crutch” and did not learn the underlying concepts deeply enough.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, different result.
What the researchers concluded

The worry is that students use a plain chatbot as a crutch. The hint-only tutor, designed to guide students instead of directly giving answers, avoided the damage. The researchers call the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later.

tiles.cap: A spacesuit, station mould, drinking water: what the crew is packing into Dragon
tiles.nums: in space, across two expeditions, for NASA’s Jessica Watkins on 31 October; the photo shows her marking it with a tray of sweets
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Monday 9 November says the Expedition 75 crew began the week packing a SpaceX Dragon cargo craft to return to Earth next week. Flight engineer Anil Menon examined colonies of bacteria, mould and fungi grown from samples swabbed off station surfaces, measured and photographed them, and packed them for return. Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney unpacked a newly delivered spacesuit, checked it and readied it for the Quest airlock, then moved another suit into Dragon so engineers on the ground can examine it.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: nearly everything that goes up must be counted, swabbed, photographed and, if it is worth the seat, brought back down.
deep: Water and breath

Canadian Space Agency flight engineer Joshua Kutryk collected samples of the station’s drinking water for microbial analysis on Earth. Roscosmos flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov recorded his breathing rate wearing an acoustic monitor around his neck, for research on how weightlessness affects the respiratory system.
Housekeeping in orbit

Station commander Pyotr Dubrov photographed mountains, volcanoes and deserts in South America and Africa. Anna Kikina checked docking mechanisms, cleaned smoke detectors and serviced life-support gear.
What NASA did not say

The blog gives no undocking or splashdown date and no mission number for this Dragon, only “next week”. The crew of seven: Dubrov, Kikina and Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the CSA.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 9 Nov 2026: Crew Packing Dragon for Return with Experiments and a Spacesuit

tiles.cap: A star 30 million light-years away flares every 113 days. X-rays found what was robbing it
tiles.nums: between the outbursts of the star AT 2016blu; at least 27 of them were recorded between 2012 and 2026
tiles.p1: For 15 years astronomers watched a star in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away, brighten like a supernova and then survive, over and over. The star, AT 2016blu, is a luminous blue variable, a type sometimes called a “supernova impostor”, with at least 33 times the Sun’s mass. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has now found the cause: a previously hidden companion, either a black hole or a neutron star, that pulls material off the star every 113 days as the two orbit each other.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA published the result on Monday 9 November; the paper is in The Astrophysical Journal.
deep: Caught at the right time

Chandra observed the star on 24 to 27 March 2026, after optical telescopes saw an outburst begin, under its “Target of Opportunity” programme. In X-rays the star was at least 100 times brighter than in 2001 to 2002, before the outbursts started. Lead author Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia: “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen.”
Why Chandra

A nearby bright X-ray source sits close to AT 2016blu on the sky, and NASA says Chandra is the only X-ray telescope with vision sharp enough to tell the two apart. The page calls this the first X-ray detection of this class of erupting star, and the first found with a black hole or neutron star companion.
Amateurs counted the bursts

The optical record came from the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Supernova Project and the American Association of Variable Star Observers, including data from more than 30 amateur astronomers. Co-author Núria Torres-Albà: “This star’s behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly it’s not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year.”
The picture
The image combines Chandra X-rays with a Sloan Digital Sky Survey optical view of NGC 4559. The best-known luminous blue variable is Eta Carinae, in our own galaxy.
tiles.src: NASA / Chandra X-ray Center, 9 Nov 2026 (Megan Watzke): NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts · The Astrophysical Journal (Aghakhanloo et al.)
tiles.credit: Image: X-ray NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; optical SDSS; processing NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Edmonds

tiles.cap: Earbuds that record what you just heard. Maker says 10 hours; the tester got 4.5 with ANC
tiles.nums: of flash memory inside Nothing’s Ear (3a) earbuds, enough to hold audio snapshots of up to a minute and call recordings
tiles.p1: Nothing’s Ear (3a) are $99 earbuds on TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list for one trick: pinch both buds and they save an “audio snapshot” of up to a minute, including up to 30 seconds of what played before you pinched, which the app can replay, transcribe or share. Inside: a 12 mm dynamic driver in each bud, Bluetooth 6.0, three directional microphones per bud, 32 MB of flash storage and an IP54 rating against dust and splashes. TechRadar’s Becky Scarrott lists one bud at 4.53 g and gave the pair 4 out of 5.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the hardware is ordinary; the argument is about what a microphone in your ear should be allowed to remember.
deep: Battery: two stories

Nothing’s launch post says up to 10 hours per charge with noise cancelling off, 6 hours with it on, and 42 hours in total with the case. TechRadar’s spec sheet gives 6 hours with ANC off, 4.5 hours with it on and 25 hours with the case; in testing the reviewer found the 4.5-hour figure “bang on”, and wrote: “In my briefing, I was told the buds themselves would last 10 hours — but that turned out not to be the case.” Battery scored 2.5 of 5.
The privacy problem

The buds can also record a phone call. Nothing says “a privacy notification alerts others when recording during a call or meeting”; TechRadar found “the only indication here that you’re being recorded may be a brief beep” and called covert recording of private conversations “a serious issue”. Its do-not-buy list: “The idea of covert surveillance bothers you.”
What worked

Noise cancelling cuts sound in the human-voice range by up to 6 dB, with peak reduction of 45 dB, says Nothing; TechRadar called the ANC “no slouch” and the sound “fun, upfront”, with LDAC support at $99 “good stuff”. Faults: no wireless charging, “a little bass-heavy at times”, and buds “a little big” for small ears.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Daniel Varghese) · Nothing launch post, Ear (3a) available now, 7 Jul 2026 · TechRadar, 25 Jul 2026 (Becky Scarrott), 4/5

tiles.cap: Chatbots raised on American English “correct” Indian English. An NUS dean weighs in
tiles.p1: Much of the language data that AI models learn from is American English, and NUS News reports that users in India have found chatbots “correcting” Indian English expressions as grammatical mistakes. Prof Lionel Wee, Dean of the NUS Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences and a sociolinguist, told a panel organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October that meaning depends on context: “Table number five wants their check” or “I’ve got to wash my hair” carry more than their words. He calls himself an “AI agnostic” and urges “a healthy dose of scepticism towards AI”.
tiles.p2: Why here: a Singapore take on the Using AI lane, from a professor who researches how people actually talk.
deep: Who was there

The panel, “Lost in Translation”, was organised by The Mandala Club on 20 October 2026. Alongside Prof Wee were Rahat Kapur, co-founder and editorial director of Beyond The Boardroom, and Chathuni Uduwela, a public policy practitioner.
Comfort from a machine

Two stories from the panel: a colleague’s niece turned to a chatbot for comfort after a breakup, and a student kept using a religious chatbot app long after exams were over. Wee’s question: “Are we creating generations that are less resilient, less able to deal with setbacks and difficulties”.
Like calculators?

NUS News’ comparison: writing reduced the need to memorise, and calculators made manual calculation less necessary. Its question: as AI takes on more thinking tasks, which human skills should we keep cultivating?
Access is not enough
Wee: “Access on its own is not really meaningful if you don’t take into account the kinds of friction that people encounter”.
